stem: This is the frontmatter of a project skill's `SKILL.md`; the body below it is empty. Claude rarely uses the skill on its own, even when someone asks for release notes. What should change?

snippet.code:
---
name: release-notes
description: >
  Step 1: run git log since the last tag.
  Step 2: group the commits by type.
  Step 3: write a summary for each group.
  Step 4: add a breaking-changes section.
  Step 5: save it to docs/RELEASE.md.
---

choices.text: Make `description` say what the skill does and when to use it, and move the steps into the body
choices.reason: Correct: Claude uses the description to decide when to apply a skill, and the body holds the instructions it follows once the skill runs.

choices.text: Move the steps into the body and delete `description`, so Claude reads the full steps before it decides
choices.reason: Without a description, Claude Code uses the body's first non-empty line instead, and the body itself loads only when the skill is used.

choices.text: Rename the skill, since Claude matches requests against the skill's `name` alone
choices.reason: `name` is the command name shown in the `/` menu. The docs say it is the `description` that Claude uses to decide when to load a skill.

choices.text: Add `disable-model-invocation: true`, so Claude loads it whenever release notes come up
choices.reason: That setting does the opposite: it stops Claude from loading the skill automatically, leaving `/release-notes` as the only way in.

takeaway: A skill's `description` is its trigger, saying what it does and when; the steps go in the body, which loads when the skill is used.
explanation: The frontmatter `description` is what Claude reads to decide whether a skill fits the request, so it should say what the skill does and when to use it. The procedure belongs in the body, which loads only when the skill runs. This description is a list of steps that never mentions release notes, so it doesn't help Claude match the request. Choice b is tempting, but the body isn't read before the decision; without a description, Claude Code just uses its first non-empty line.

stem: A client connects to this MCP server, built with the Python SDK, and lists its tools. What does the client receive for `lookup_order`?

snippet.code:
from mcp.server import MCPServer

mcp = MCPServer("orders")

@mcp.tool()
async def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up an order's status and ETA.

    Args:
        order_id: Order number, e.g. A-1042
    """
    order = await db.get(order_id)
    return f"{order.status}, ETA {order.eta}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

choices.text: A definition built from the code: the docstring as its description and a schema with a string `order_id`
choices.reason: Correct: `MCPServer` uses Python type hints and docstrings to generate tool definitions automatically, so the docstring and `order_id: str` shape what the client gets.

choices.text: The function's source code, so the model can read exactly what the tool does before calling it
choices.reason: The server sends a tool definition generated from the type hints and docstring. The function body is the handler that runs when the tool is called.

choices.text: Only the name `lookup_order`; the description has to be written separately in each client's configuration file
choices.reason: The docstring already supplies the description: `MCPServer` builds tool definitions from type hints and docstrings, so no separate description is needed.

choices.text: A schema that accepts any value for `order_id`, because Python ignores type hints at runtime
choices.reason: `MCPServer` reads the type hints to generate the tool definition, so `order_id: str` becomes a string parameter in the schema.

takeaway: In a Python MCP server, the type hints and docstring **are** the tool definition, so write them for the model that will read them.
explanation: The Python SDK's `MCPServer` turns each `@mcp.tool()` function into a tool definition automatically, reading the type hints for the input schema and the docstring for the description. That generated definition, not the code, is what the client receives; the body runs only when the tool is called. Choice c is tempting if you have written raw tool schemas before, but here the docstring is the description.

stem: Your MCP server's SDK turns this docstring into the tool's description. The tool searches your support knowledge base, but Claude rarely calls it for how-to questions, and when it does it passes the user's whole message as `q`. What is the best first fix?

choices.text: Add a second tool, `find`, with the same docstring, so Claude has two chances to pick a search
choices.reason: Overlap makes it worse: when tools overlap in function or have a vague purpose, agents can get confused about which ones to use.

choices.text: Shorten the docstring to `"KB."`, because every word of a description costs context on each turn
choices.reason: The problem is ambiguity, not length. Describe the tool as you would to a new hire; even small refinements to descriptions can yield dramatic improvements.

choices.text: Rewrite the docstring to say what it searches, when to use it and what to pass, and give `q` a clear name
choices.reason: Correct: prompt-engineering tool descriptions is one of the most effective ways to improve tools. Explain it as you would to a new hire, and name inputs unambiguously.

choices.text: Raise an exception with the full traceback whenever nothing matches, so Claude can learn what the tool covers
choices.reason: Error responses should give specific, actionable guidance rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks, and an error wouldn't change when Claude picks the tool.

takeaway: When Claude misuses a tool, fix its description and parameter names first, written as you would brief a new hire.
explanation: The description `"Search."` doesn't say what is searched, when the tool fits, or what `q` should hold, so Claude can't match it to how-to questions or fill the input well. Anthropic calls prompt-engineering tool descriptions one of the most effective ways to improve tools, along with unambiguous parameter names like `user_id` instead of `user`. Choice b is tempting as a context saving, but the failure here is ambiguity, not length.

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

stem: This MCP server passes its unit tests, which call `lookup_order` directly. When Claude Code launches it as a local stdio server, the connection breaks as soon as the tool is called. What is the cause?

snippet.code:
mcp = MCPServer("orders")

@mcp.tool()
async def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up an order's status by order ID."""
    print(f"lookup_order called: {order_id}")
    order = await db.get(order_id)
    return order.status

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

choices.text: `print()` writes to stdout, which carries the JSON-RPC messages; log to stderr with the `logging` module
choices.reason: Correct: on a stdio server, writing to stdout corrupts the JSON-RPC messages and breaks the server. The standard `logging` module writes to stderr instead.

choices.text: The `print()` call needs `flush=True`, so the log line reaches stdout in one piece
choices.reason: Any write to stdout corrupts the JSON-RPC messages on a stdio server; flushing just sends the stray text sooner. Keep `print()` out of the server entirely.

choices.text: Tools on a stdio server can't be `async`, so change `async def` to plain `def` so each call returns in time
choices.reason: The guide's own stdio weather server defines its tools with `async def`, so async handlers are fine.

choices.text: A stdio tool has to return a dict, so wrap `order.status` in `{"status": ...}`
choices.reason: The guide's stdio tools return plain strings, so returning a `str` is not the problem.

takeaway: A stdio MCP server's stdout belongs to the protocol: send every log line to stderr.
explanation: On a stdio server, stdout carries the JSON-RPC messages, so the stray `print()` output corrupts them the moment the tool runs. Unit tests that call the function directly never notice. Logging through Python's `logging` module goes to stderr instead and leaves the protocol intact. Choice b is tempting, but flushing only delivers the corrupting text sooner.

stem: When the requested room is already taken, your MCP server's `book_room` tool sends this response. Your agent's logs count these as successful bookings. What should the server change?

choices.text: Return a JSON-RPC `error` object with code `-32602` instead of a result
choices.reason: Protocol errors cover problems with the request itself, such as an unknown tool or a malformed request. A taken room is a business logic error, which goes in the result.

choices.text: Add an `outputSchema` to `book_room` so the client can validate the result
choices.reason: An output schema lets clients validate the structure of structured results; it doesn't mark a call as failed.

choices.text: Send `notifications/tools/list_changed` so the client lists the tools again
choices.reason: That notification tells clients that the list of available tools has changed; it says nothing about the outcome of one call.

choices.text: Keep the message in `content` and set `isError` to `true`
choices.reason: Correct: tool execution errors, including business logic errors, are reported in the tool result with `isError: true`, and the message gives the model actionable feedback.

takeaway: A tool that ran but failed returns a result with `isError: true`; JSON-RPC errors are for problems with the request itself.
explanation: MCP has two error channels. Protocol errors (unknown tool, malformed request, server errors) are JSON-RPC `error` objects; tool execution errors such as API failures, input validation errors and business logic errors come back as a normal result with `isError: true`. This response describes a failure but flags it as a success. Choice a is tempting because something did go wrong, but the request itself was fine.

stem: Your agent uses this tool to read a customer's past invoices. Claude often skips it when it should call it, and when it does call it, `range` arrives in several different date formats. Which two changes to the definition help most?

choices.text: Shorten the description further so the tool costs fewer input tokens on every request
choices.reason: The docs call detailed descriptions by far the most important factor in tool performance. A shorter one gives Claude even less to go on.

choices.text: Rewrite the description to say what the tool returns, when to use it and when not to
choices.reason: Correct: a description should cover what the tool does, when it should (and shouldn't) be used and its caveats, aiming for at least 3 to 4 sentences.

choices.text: Copy the description into the system prompt so Claude also sees it there
choices.reason: The API already builds a tool-use system prompt from your tool definitions. The fix is a better description inside the definition itself.

choices.text: Give `id` and `range` their own descriptions, saying what each means and its format
choices.reason: Correct: the docs say to explain what each parameter means and how it affects the tool, as the good example does for `ticker` ("e.g. AAPL").

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` so Claude has to call a tool on every turn
choices.reason: `any` makes Claude call some tool every turn, even when none fits. It tells Claude nothing about what `range` should look like.

takeaway: Tool quality rides on the description: what it does, when to use it, and what each parameter means and looks like.
explanation: Claude chooses and fills a tool only from its definition. "Gets data." says nothing about invoices or when to reach for the tool, and the bare `range` string gives no format, so Claude guesses. The two fixes put that missing context into the tool and parameter descriptions. Forcing a call with `tool_choice` is tempting because it stops the skipping, but it makes Claude call a tool even when none is needed and still leaves `range` undefined.

stem: A teammate ported this tool definition from another provider's SDK and added it to the `tools` array of a Messages API request. Which change makes it a valid Claude tool definition?

choices.text: Add `"strict": true` so Claude validates its inputs against `parameters`
choices.reason: `strict` turns on schema validation for tool inputs, but the schema it checks against is `input_schema`. It doesn't make another key a schema.

choices.text: Wrap the object in `{"type": "function", "function": {...}}` first
choices.reason: A user-defined Claude tool is a plain entry in `tools` with `name`, `description` and `input_schema`. There's no function wrapper.

choices.text: Rename the `parameters` key to `input_schema`
choices.reason: Correct: a Claude tool definition puts its JSON Schema for the expected parameters in `input_schema`.

choices.text: Move the parameter details into `description` and delete the schema object
choices.reason: The description explains the tool, but `input_schema` is the JSON Schema that defines the parameters. Dropping it removes the schema.

takeaway: A Claude tool is `name`, `description` and `input_schema`; schemas ported from other APIs usually need that key renamed.
explanation: The definition is fine except for one key: Claude tools carry their parameter schema in `input_schema`. Other providers' formats use `parameters` or a `function` wrapper, which is why ported definitions trip on this. Adding `strict` is tempting because it sounds like stricter checking, but strict mode validates inputs against `input_schema`, so it doesn't help when that key is missing.

stem: This loop runs the tools Claude asks for, but the API rejects the second request, complaining about the tool results. What is wrong with the code?

snippet.code:
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools, messages=messages)
while resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    results = []
    for block in resp.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": out})
    messages.append(
        {"role": "user", "content": results})
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools, messages=messages)

choices.text: It never appends Claude's turn (`resp.content`) before the results
choices.reason: Correct: each `tool_result` must come right after the assistant message holding its `tool_use` block. Here that message is missing from the history.

choices.text: `tool_use_id` should be the ID of the whole response message, not of the block
choices.reason: `tool_use_id` is the `id` of the `tool_use` block the result answers, which is what `block.id` already is.

choices.text: The results belong in an `assistant` message, because Claude is the one who asked
choices.reason: Tool results go in a `user` message; `assistant` messages hold Claude's own content, including its `tool_use` blocks.

choices.text: Each `tool_result` needs a text block before it saying which tool produced it
choices.reason: `tool_result` blocks must come first in the user message, with any text after them. A text block in front would cause its own error.

takeaway: Append Claude's full turn before your tool results: every `tool_result` must directly follow the `tool_use` it answers.
explanation: The tool results are formatted correctly. What's missing is the message they answer: the code adds a user message of results to a history that has no assistant turn with those `tool_use` IDs. Appending `{"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}` before the results fixes it. Choice b is tempting because an ID mismatch gives a similar error, but `block.id` is exactly the right ID.

stem: Claude asks for two tools in one response, and this code runs both. The next request fails because the results don't match the tool calls. Which change fixes it?

choices.text: Push the assistant turn after the tool results instead of before them
choices.reason: Tool results must come right after the assistant message that holds the `tool_use` blocks, so the current order is already right.

choices.text: Keep `res.id`, and add `is_error: false` to each result to mark it as a success
choices.reason: `is_error` is optional and only set to `true` when a tool fails. It doesn't change which call a result answers.

choices.text: Convert `out` to a list of text blocks, since `content` can't be a plain string
choices.reason: A `tool_result` `content` may be a plain string such as `"15 degrees"`, so the string isn't the problem.

choices.text: Set `tool_use_id` to `block.id` for each result
choices.reason: Correct: `tool_use_id` is the `id` of the `tool_use` block. `res.id` is the whole message's ID, and here both results share it.

takeaway: `tool_use_id` copies the `id` of the `tool_use` block, never the response's message ID.
explanation: Each `tool_use` block has its own `id`, and each `tool_result` matches its call by echoing that `id` in `tool_use_id`. The code uses `res.id`, the ID of the whole response, so neither result matches a call, and the two results carry the same ID. The rest of the loop (assistant turn first, results in one user message, string content) is already correct, which is why the other changes don't help.

stem: Claude often asks for `get_weather` and `get_time` in the same response, and your loop handles them as shown. As the conversation goes on, Claude makes fewer and fewer parallel calls. What should change?

snippet.code:
messages.append({"role": "assistant",
                 "content": resp.content})
for block in resp.content:
    if block.type != "tool_use":
        continue
    out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "tool_result",
         "tool_use_id": block.id,
         "content": out}]})
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools, messages=messages)

choices.text: Run the tools concurrently with `asyncio.gather` instead of one after another
choices.reason: The API leaves execution order to you, so sequential runs are fine. The problem is how the results are laid out in the history.

choices.text: Send all the `tool_result` blocks together in one user message
choices.reason: Correct: return one `tool_result` per `tool_use`, all together in the next user message. A separate message per result "teaches" Claude to avoid parallel calls.

choices.text: Put a short text block before each `tool_result` saying which tool produced it
choices.reason: Every `tool_result` must come before any text in the user message, and `tool_use_id` already ties each result to its call.

choices.text: Leave the assistant turn out of the history, since each result already names its call
choices.reason: The results answer the `tool_use` blocks in that assistant turn, so it has to stay in the history right before them.

takeaway: Parallel calls get their results back together: one user message holding every `tool_result`.
explanation: Each result here is correct on its own, with the right `tool_use_id`. The trouble is the shape of the history: one user message per result. The docs name this as the most common reason parallel tool use fades, because the history shows Claude a pattern of one call at a time. Choice a is tempting because it sounds like "more parallel", but how you run the tools doesn't matter to Claude; how you return the results does.

stem: Claude asks for three tools in one turn, and one of them raises an exception in this code. Which two statements about the code, and how to fix it, are correct?

snippet.code:
results = []
for block in resp.content:
    if block.type != "tool_use":
        continue
    try:
        out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
    except Exception:
        continue  # skip failed calls
    results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": block.id,
                    "content": out})
messages.append({"role": "assistant",
                 "content": resp.content})
messages.append({"role": "user",
                 "content": results})

choices.text: The next request can fail, because one `tool_use` block now has no matching `tool_result`
choices.reason: Correct: every `tool_use` needs its `tool_result` right after it. The docs quote the error "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after".

choices.text: Claude treats the missing result as an empty success and carries on with the other two
choices.reason: An empty result is a `tool_result` sent without `content`. Leaving the result out altogether breaks the pairing the API expects.

choices.text: In the `except` branch, add a `tool_result` for that ID with the error text and `"is_error": true`
choices.reason: Correct: when a tool throws, return the error message in `content` with `"is_error": true`, and Claude can work the failure into its reply.

choices.text: Mark the failure by setting `is_error` on Claude's `tool_use` block in the assistant turn
choices.reason: `is_error` is a field of the `tool_result` block you send back, not of Claude's `tool_use` block.

choices.text: Use `"content": "failed"` for the error, since more detail would only distract Claude
choices.reason: The docs say to write instructive errors: what went wrong and what to try next, such as "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."

takeaway: A failed tool still gets a `tool_result`: the error text with `is_error: true`, never a skipped block.
explanation: Skipping the failed call leaves a `tool_use` with nothing answering it, which is the formatting error the docs warn about. The fix is to answer it anyway, with `is_error: true` and an error message that says what went wrong, so Claude can explain the failure or try something else. Choice b is the tempting assumption that silence means "no output", but no result and an empty result are different things.

stem: This loop keeps calling Claude until it stops asking for tools. Which line belongs at `# ???`?

snippet.code:
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant",
                     "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = [
        {"type": "tool_result",
         "tool_use_id": b.id,
         "content": run_tool(b.name, b.input)}
        for b in resp.content
        if b.type == "tool_use"
    ]
    # ???

choices.text: `messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": results})`
choices.reason: The Claude API has no `tool` role. Tool results travel inside the ordinary `user` and `assistant` message structure.

choices.text: `messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": results})`
choices.reason: `assistant` messages hold Claude's own content and `tool_use` blocks. Your tool results belong to the other side of the conversation.

choices.text: `messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})`
choices.reason: Correct: tool results go back in a new `user` message, right after the assistant turn that called the tools.

choices.text: `messages[0]["content"] += str(results)`
choices.reason: Results must immediately follow their `tool_use` blocks as `tool_result` blocks. Pasting them into the first message breaks that.

takeaway: Tool output goes back as `tool_result` blocks in a `user` message, right after Claude's tool-calling turn.
explanation: The loop already saves Claude's turn, stops when there's nothing left to run and builds well-formed `tool_result` blocks. The missing step is sending them: a new `user` message, so the next `create` call sees the call and its result side by side. Choice a is the tempting carry-over from APIs that use a dedicated `tool` or `function` role; Claude's API doesn't have one.

stem: This request forces Claude to call `record_summary`. The `print` line then fails because `content[0]` has no `text`. Why?

snippet.code:
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[record_summary_tool],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool",
                 "name": "record_summary"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": doc}],
)
print(resp.content[0].text)

choices.text: A forced call starts the response with the `tool_use` block, no text first
choices.reason: Correct: with `tool` or `any`, the API prefills the turn so Claude won't write text before the `tool_use` block. Read `input` from that block.

choices.text: Claude ran `record_summary` itself, so `content[0]` holds the tool's output
choices.reason: The response holds a `tool_use` block with the `input` Claude chose for the call, not the result of running the tool.

choices.text: Naming one tool is only a hint, so Claude declined and returned a refusal block
choices.reason: `{"type": "tool"}` forces Claude to always use that tool. It isn't a suggestion Claude can turn down.

choices.text: `max_tokens` is too low, so the reply stopped before Claude wrote its text
choices.reason: A cut-off reply reports `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. With a forced call, there is no text before the `tool_use` block at all.

takeaway: With a forced `tool_choice`, expect no preamble: find the `tool_use` block by type and read its `input`.
explanation: Forcing a tool (`tool` or `any`) makes the API prefill Claude's turn so it goes straight into the tool call: no text explanation first, even if you ask for one. So `content[0]` is the `tool_use` block, which has `input` but no `text`. Choice b is tempting because the tool is named, but the API doesn't run your tool: the block carries the `input` Claude chose, and your code runs it. Find blocks by `type`, not by position.

stem: Your support bot sends requests like this one. Even for small talk such as "Thanks, bye!", Claude calls `lookup_order` instead of simply replying. Real order questions should still use the tool. Which change fixes it?

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "none"}`, so Claude stops calling tools it doesn't need
choices.reason: `none` stops Claude using any tools, so real order questions could no longer call `lookup_order` either.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "auto"}`, so Claude decides whether a tool is needed
choices.reason: Correct: `auto` lets Claude choose whether to call a tool, and it's the default when tools are provided. `any` requires a tool call every time.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "lookup_order"}` to narrow it
choices.reason: `tool` forces Claude to always use that tool, so small talk would still trigger a lookup.

choices.text: Keep `any`, and tell Claude in the system prompt to skip tools for small talk
choices.reason: With `any`, the API prefills the turn to force a tool call, so a prompt instruction can't turn that call off.

takeaway: `any` means "always call some tool"; `auto` lets Claude decide, which is what a chat assistant needs.
explanation: The request sets `tool_choice` to `any`, which tells Claude it must use one of the provided tools on every response. A message that needs no lookup still gets one. `auto` restores Claude's judgment. Option d is tempting because prompts usually steer tool use, but with `any` the API forces the tool call before Claude writes anything.

stem: An agent that handles product returns fails on its first tool call. Read the trace. Identify the mechanism and choose the targeted fix.

snippet.code:
SESSION TRACE  (returns assistant, turn 3)
T3 assistant:
  text: "Let me look up that return."
  tool_use  id=toolu_01Kp7  name=get_return
            input={"rma":"R-5520"}
[app] get_return -> 180 chars (ok)
T3 user:
  tool_result  tool_use_id=toolu_01Kq9
               content="status: received ..."
[api] 400 invalid_request_error:
  tool_result id has no matching tool_use

choices.text: The result's `tool_use_id` doesn't match the id Claude issued; set it to `toolu_01Kp7` so the result pairs with its call
choices.reason: Correct: `tool_use_id` is "the id of the tool use request this is a result for", and the `id` on each `tool_use` block "will be used to match up the tool results later".

choices.text: The tool description doesn't say what it returns; add a return-format sentence so Claude issues the call correctly
choices.reason: Claude picked the right tool with a valid input and the tool ran fine. The failure is in how the app formatted the result, not in the tool's description.

choices.text: A `tool_result` must also name the tool; add `name: get_return` to the block so the API can pair it with the call
choices.reason: A `tool_result` carries `tool_use_id`, optional `content` and optional `is_error`. There is no `name` field; pairing is done by id alone.

choices.text: The text block before the `tool_use` confused the API; strip text blocks from assistant turns before replaying them in history
choices.reason: An assistant turn with a `text` block followed by a `tool_use` block is the documented normal shape; it is not what the 400 is about.

takeaway: A `tool_result` is paired with its call by `tool_use_id`; copy the `id` from the `tool_use` block Claude returned.
explanation: The integration layer, not the model, broke here: the assistant turn issued `toolu_01Kp7`, the app replied with `toolu_01Kq9`, and the API rejected a result that matches no call. The fix is to carry the exact `id` from the `tool_use` block into `tool_use_id`. Options b and c are traps because they fix the schema layer, which worked: Claude chose the right tool with a valid input.

stem: Claude requested two tools in one turn. One lookup timed out, and the app's loop only returns results for calls that succeeded. Read the trace. What is the mechanism, and what should change?

snippet.code:
SESSION TRACE  (travel agent, turn 2)
T2 assistant:  stop_reason=tool_use
  tool_use id=toolu_0A1 name=get_flights
  tool_use id=toolu_0A2 name=get_hotels
[app] get_flights -> 1,900 chars
[app] get_hotels  -> TimeoutError (skipped)
T2 user:
  tool_result tool_use_id=toolu_0A1 ...
[api] 400 invalid_request_error:
  tool_use ids were found without
  tool_result blocks immediately after

choices.text: The hotel call ran too long; raise `max_tokens` so Claude has room to wait for both lookups before it continues
choices.reason: `max_tokens` caps the length of Claude's output. It has nothing to do with the app's timeout or with the result block that was never sent.

choices.text: Two tool calls in one turn aren't allowed; set `disable_parallel_tool_use` so the loop only ever has to handle one call at a time
choices.reason: Several `tool_use` blocks in one response are normal. Serialising them hides the real bug: the next timeout would still leave a call unanswered.

choices.text: Every `tool_use` needs a `tool_result` in that user message; add one for `toolu_0A2` with the error text and `is_error: true`
choices.reason: Correct: this error means a `tool_use` had no result; the page's fix for a failing tool is a `tool_result` carrying the error message with `"is_error": true`, so Claude can react.

choices.text: Send the hotel result later, in a follow-up user message after Claude's next reply, once the retry succeeds
choices.reason: "Tool result blocks must immediately follow their corresponding tool use blocks"; no messages may sit between the tool-use turn and its results.

takeaway: Answer every tool call in the same user message, and report failures with `is_error: true` instead of skipping them.
explanation: The loop violated the tool-use contract: both `tool_use` blocks from one assistant turn must be answered in the immediately following user message, and a failed tool is reported, not omitted. Sending a `tool_result` for `toolu_0A2` with the timeout text and `is_error: true` satisfies the API and lets Claude recover. Option b is the trap: disabling parallel calls removes the symptom this time but leaves the same bug for the next failure.

stem: Your team has a 40-step database-migration procedure that's needed a few times a quarter. Claude should pick it up on its own whenever someone asks to migrate a table, and it shouldn't cost context the rest of the time. Which packaging fits, and why?

choices.text: CLAUDE.md, because Claude can only follow instructions that are already loaded into every session it starts
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md content loads every session. A skill's body loads only when it's used, and its description lets Claude load it automatically when relevant.

choices.text: A plugin, because any procedure that comes with supporting files has to be distributed as a plugin
choices.reason: Skills work on their own: a skill directory can hold supporting files, and a project skill in `.claude/skills/` loads for everyone who clones the repo.

choices.text: A skill in `.claude/skills/`: its description says when to use it, and its body loads only when used
choices.reason: Correct: Claude uses skills when relevant, deciding from the `description`, and unlike CLAUDE.md the body costs nothing until the skill runs.

choices.text: A skill with `disable-model-invocation: true`, because a long procedure should only ever run when typed by name
choices.reason: That setting stops Claude loading the skill on its own, so people would have to type `/migrate` each time. The scenario wants Claude to pick it up when the task matches.

takeaway: An occasional procedure Claude should recognise on its own is a skill: a matching `description`, a body that loads on demand.
explanation: The decision rule is loading behaviour. A skill's description is what Claude matches a task against, and its body enters context only when used, which fits a long, occasional procedure. Choice d is the tempting near miss: it is also a skill, but `disable-model-invocation: true` is for workflows you trigger manually, and this one should trigger when the task matches.

stem: A platform team wants to enable a plugin with 12 skills, two hooks and an MCP server for every developer. Which two are true of what the enabled plugin adds to each developer's sessions?

choices.text: The name and description of each skill Claude can invoke on its own sit in context on every turn, even in sessions that never use the plugin
choices.reason: Correct: for each skill, agent and command Claude can invoke on its own, the name and description are in context on every turn, and those tokens count toward usage.

choices.text: The full text of all 12 skills is loaded at session start, so the plugin's context cost is fixed and known up front
choices.reason: The full text of a skill or agent loads only when it's used; only names and descriptions are present on every turn.

choices.text: Its MCP server runs alongside every session where the plugin is enabled, and its hooks fire at their events
choices.reason: Correct: MCP servers the plugin defines run alongside each session where it's enabled, and its hooks fire at their events, whether or not a skill from the plugin is used.

choices.text: Its hooks fire only in sessions where someone invokes one of the plugin's skills
choices.reason: Hooks fire at their lifecycle events in every enabled session; invoking a skill isn't what arms them.

choices.text: What the plugin runs is sandboxed away from the developer's own permissions
choices.reason: What a plugin runs, it runs as you, with your user privileges, which is why the docs say to review a plugin's security before installing it.

takeaway: An enabled plugin is part of every session: descriptions in context each turn, servers running, hooks armed; only skill bodies wait until used.
explanation: The overview separates what a plugin costs every session from what loads on demand. Names and descriptions of invocable skills, agents and commands are in context on every turn (a), and the plugin's MCP servers run and its hooks fire wherever it's enabled (c). Choice b overstates the cost: full skill text loads only when used. Choice e understates the risk: plugin code runs as you.

diagram.caption: Per turn, only names and descriptions are in context; bodies load when used.

stem: Your team uploaded a custom reporting skill and sends this Messages API request. A reviewer says the skill can't run as written. What's missing?

choices.text: A `settingSources` entry so the API discovers the skill from the project's `.claude/skills/` folder
choices.reason: `settingSources` is an Agent SDK option for loading filesystem settings; the Messages API reads no folders on your machine. The skill is already uploaded and named by `skill_id`.

choices.text: A `SKILL.md` upload through the Files API, attached with a container upload block
choices.reason: Files API uploads are input files for a skill to work on. The skill itself is uploaded through the Skills API, which this team already did; the `skill_id` proves it.

choices.text: The skill's instructions copied into `system`, since the container only holds its scripts
choices.reason: Claude loads a skill's full instructions only when needed, from the skill files copied into the container; pasting them into `system` isn't part of the integration.

choices.text: The code execution tool in `tools`, because Skills run in its container and require it
choices.reason: Correct: Skills integrate with the Messages API through the code execution tool, which is required; pre-built and custom skills both use the same `container` structure alongside it.

takeaway: On the API a skill is `container.skills` plus the code execution tool; it is uploaded once, not pasted into `system` or read from disk.
explanation: Skills on the API run inside the code execution container, so the request must enable the code execution tool as well as naming the skill in `container.skills`. The snippet has the container entry but no `tools` array, which is the defect (d). Choice a is the wrong layer: `settingSources` is how the Agent SDK finds skills on disk. Choice b confuses the Files API (input files) with the Skills API (the skill itself).

stem: A scheduled job runs this Agent SDK query on a CI runner, inside a checkout of the repo whose `.claude/skills/nightly-triage/SKILL.md` holds the procedure. The runner's service account has no skills of its own. Which value fills the blank so the skill is discovered?

choices.text: `"user"`
choices.reason: `user` loads the `~/.claude/` of the account running the job, which holds no skills here. The repo's skills are project skills.

choices.text: `"project"`
choices.reason: Correct: project skills live in `<cwd>/.claude/skills/`, and the SDK loads them only when `settingSources` includes `'project'`. Set explicitly without it, the SDK doesn't load them.

choices.text: `"local"`
choices.reason: Skills are discovered through the `user` and `project` setting sources; `local` isn't one of the sources skills come from.

choices.text: `"all"`
choices.reason: `"all"` is a value of the `skills` option, which decides which already-discovered skills Claude may invoke. It isn't a setting source and discovers nothing by itself.

takeaway: In the SDK, a repo's skills come through the `project` setting source; an explicit `settingSources` list that omits it loads none of them.
explanation: The SDK discovers skills through filesystem setting sources: `user` for `~/.claude/skills/` and `project` for `.claude/skills/` under the working directory. The skill in this job is in the checkout, so `project` is the source that finds it (b). Choice d mixes up two options: `skills: "all"` only controls which already-discovered skills Claude can invoke; it discovers nothing by itself.

stem: A release-notes skill works in a developer's Claude Code sessions; its step 2 runs a script from `~/tools/` on his laptop. You're attaching the skill to a Claude Managed Agent, which Anthropic hosts and your services reach by agent ID. What must change?

choices.text: Nothing: when a session starts, the hosted agent reads the attached skill and its script from the developer's machine
choices.reason: Custom skills are uploaded to the workspace as a directory holding `SKILL.md` plus supporting files and attached by `skill_id`; a hosted session never sees a developer's machine.

choices.text: Add the laptop's `~/tools/` path to the agent's allowed directories so the sandbox can reach the script
choices.reason: The sandbox is Anthropic-hosted; there is no laptop path to allow. Supporting files travel inside the uploaded skill or in a repository mounted on the session.

choices.text: Rewrite step 2 to use a script bundled in the uploaded skill, because the hosted sandbox can't see his laptop
choices.reason: Correct: a custom skill is a directory containing `SKILL.md` plus any supporting files, uploaded to your workspace; the agent reads the skill, including any scripts it ships, inside the session's sandbox.

choices.text: Replace the skill with a `.claude/commands/` file, since hosted agents run commands but can't load skills
choices.reason: Managed Agents take skills, attached by `skill_id` or discovered in a mounted repository's `.claude/skills`; the fix is to make the skill self-contained, not to change its format.

takeaway: A skill for a hosted agent must carry everything it needs: scripts and resources ship inside the skill, never on someone's machine.
explanation: The decision rule is where the skill actually runs. A Managed Agent runs in an Anthropic-hosted sandbox, so a step that reaches for a file on a developer's laptop has nothing to find; the script has to travel inside the uploaded skill bundle (or a mounted repository). Choice b is the trap: it treats the sandbox like a local process whose filesystem you can widen, but there is no path from the hosted session to the laptop.

stem: A teammate wrote this project skill. It works on her machine and fails for everyone else who runs it. Which part is the defect?

snippet.code:
.claude/skills/link-check/SKILL.md
---
name: link-check
description: Find broken links before a release.
---
1. Build the docs site with `npm run build`.
2. Run the checker:
   python /home/priya/docs-site/tools/links.py
3. Fix each broken link it reports.
4. Summarize what changed for the user.

choices.text: Step 2 runs the script by an absolute path under one person's home directory
choices.reason: Correct: `/home/priya/...` exists only on her machine. The docs provide `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` and `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` so a skill can reference scripts independent of where it's installed.

choices.text: The skill is under `.claude/skills/` instead of `.claude/commands/`, so `/link-check` is never created
choices.reason: Both locations create `/link-check` and work the same way; custom commands were merged into skills.

choices.text: The frontmatter lacks `disable-model-invocation`, so Claude can't load the skill on its own
choices.reason: That field defaults to `false`: Claude loads a skill automatically when its description matches. Setting it to `true` would make the skill manual-only.

choices.text: The description says when to use the skill, which belongs in the body instead
choices.reason: The description is meant to say what the skill does and when to use it; that's what Claude matches a task against.

takeaway: A skill that only works on its author's machine usually hard-codes a path; reference scripts through `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` or `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.
explanation: The symptom, works for the author and fails for everyone else, points at something machine-specific, and the only such thing here is the absolute path in step 2 (a). The other parts follow the docs: skills in `.claude/skills/` create the command, Claude may invoke a skill unless `disable-model-invocation` is set, and the description should include when to use it. Choice c inverts what that field does.

stem: You've found the defect in the `link-check` skill: step 2 runs `python /home/priya/docs-site/tools/links.py`. The script is committed in the repo at `tools/links.py`, outside the skill folder. Which rewrite fixes the step on every machine?

choices.text: `python /opt/shared-tools/links.py`, after asking everyone to copy the script there
choices.reason: That moves the assumption instead of removing it: still a machine-specific absolute path, plus a manual setup step the repository can't enforce.

choices.text: `python ~/docs-site/tools/links.py`
choices.reason: `~` expands to each user's home directory, and the checkout isn't necessarily there: it lives wherever each person cloned the repository.

choices.text: `python ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/links.py`
choices.reason: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is the directory holding `SKILL.md`, for scripts bundled inside the skill. This script lives in the repo's `tools/`, not in the skill folder.

choices.text: `python ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/tools/links.py`
choices.reason: Correct: `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` is the project root, so the step finds the repo's script on any machine, independent of where the skill is installed.

takeaway: Reference project files through `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` and skill-bundled files through `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`; never a path from one machine.
explanation: The fix must name the script relative to something every machine shares. The script is part of the repository, so the project root is that anchor: `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` resolves to it wherever the checkout lives (d). Choice c is the near miss: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is right for files shipped inside the skill folder, which this script isn't. Choices a and b just move the hard-coded assumption.

stem: A data engineer wrote a CSV-profiling MCP server that she runs only on her own laptop, in one project. Which transport and scope fit?

choices.text: `stdio` + local scope
choices.reason: Correct: stdio servers run as local processes on your machine, and local scope, the default, loads a server only in the project where you added it and keeps it private to you.

choices.text: `HTTP` + project scope (`.mcp.json`)
choices.reason: HTTP is the transport for remote servers, and project scope commits the entry to `.mcp.json` so the whole team gets it. Neither matches a personal local tool.

choices.text: `HTTP` + managed configuration
choices.reason: Managed configuration is how administrators deploy servers to every user in an organization, the opposite of one person's own tool.

choices.text: `stdio` + project scope
choices.reason: stdio is right for a local process, but project scope writes the server into the repo's `.mcp.json` for every teammate, which she doesn't want.

takeaway: Personal, local, one project: run it over stdio at local scope, the default.
explanation: Transport follows where the server runs: a process on your own machine is stdio. Scope follows who should load it: just you, in this project, is local scope, which is also the default when you add a server. Choice d is tempting because the transport is right, but project scope shares the server through a committed file, which this engineer doesn't want.

stem: Your company hosts an API-catalog MCP server at an internal URL. Everyone who clones the backend repo should get it without any setup. Which transport and scope fit?

choices.text: `stdio` + project scope (`.mcp.json`)
choices.reason: stdio runs a local process on each machine. This server is hosted remotely at a URL, so Claude Code should connect to it over HTTP.

choices.text: `HTTP` + local scope (`~/.claude.json`)
choices.reason: Local scope keeps the server private to you in one project; teammates who clone the repo wouldn't get it.

choices.text: `HTTP` + project scope
choices.reason: Correct: HTTP is the recommended transport for remote servers, and project-scoped servers live in `.mcp.json` at the project root, checked in so everyone on the team gets the same tools.

choices.text: `HTTP` + user scope (`~/.claude.json`)
choices.reason: User scope makes a server available across all your projects but private to your account; it's stored in `~/.claude.json`, not shared through the repo.

takeaway: Remote server, whole team, this repo: HTTP transport, project scope, `.mcp.json` committed.
explanation: Two independent choices. The server is reached at a URL, so the transport is HTTP. The requirement that every cloner gets it with no setup points at project scope, whose `.mcp.json` travels with the repository. Choice d is the common slip: user scope sounds like "for people", but it means all of your projects, private to you.

stem: Two MCP servers are being set up: a PDF-parsing prototype one developer is still experimenting with, and a license-audit server the platform team wants in every developer's Claude Code. Which two placements are right?

choices.text: Parser: local scope, over stdio or HTTP, so it stays in that developer's project until it's ready
choices.reason: Correct: local scope is for personal development servers and experimental configurations; the transport is a separate choice.

choices.text: Parser: project scope, so teammates can try it as soon as it's committed
choices.reason: Project scope checks the entry into `.mcp.json` for the whole team, which is sharing a server that isn't ready to share.

choices.text: Audit server: deployed by administrators through managed configuration, so every user receives it
choices.reason: Correct: administrators deploy or provide servers for every user through managed configuration, which is how a server reaches the whole organization.

choices.text: Audit server: each developer adds it at user scope, which covers all of their projects
choices.reason: User scope reaches all of one person's projects but is private to that account; it relies on every developer adding it themselves.

choices.text: Audit server: project scope in each repository's `.mcp.json`, since committed files reach every developer
choices.reason: A `.mcp.json` reaches only the people working in that repository, one repo at a time; it isn't an organization-wide deployment.

takeaway: Not ready to share: local scope. Required for everyone: admin-managed configuration, not a scope each person opts into.
explanation: Scope answers "who should load this server?". A prototype belongs to one person in one project, so local scope, whatever its transport (a). A server the whole organization must have is deployed by administrators through managed configuration rather than added by each user (c). Choice d is tempting because user scope sounds wide, but it widens one person's reach across projects; it doesn't reach other people.

stem: Your team's plugin goes into its private marketplace tomorrow. A teammate says it's ready because it works when she loads it with `--plugin-dir` from her checkout. What is still missing before the first release?

choices.text: Nothing: loading the folder with `--plugin-dir` exercises the same path an install from the marketplace will take
choices.reason: A folder load skips the catalog entirely. The name, the version, validation and an install from a marketplace are what decide whether a release works for the people who install it.

choices.text: A review in Anthropic's developer portal, because every marketplace release is checked there before users can see it
choices.reason: Your own marketplace publishes the moment the file is in the repository, with no submission form; the developer portal is for Anthropic's directory.

choices.text: A `.zip` of the plugin attached to the release, so users have a copy to fall back on if the marketplace fails
choices.reason: Sending a folder or `.zip` is the no-marketplace route, and people who load it get no updates; marketplace users update with a command instead.

choices.text: A validation pass and an install from a local marketplace, which are what decide whether a release works
choices.reason: Correct: before a release, run `claude plugin validate --strict`, then add a local marketplace that lists the plugin, install from it and start a session to confirm it loads.

takeaway: A plugin is release-ready when it validates and installs from a marketplace, not when it loads from a folder.
explanation: Readiness is judged on the path users will take: they install from a catalog, so the release has to validate and install from a marketplace, which a `--plugin-dir` load never exercises. Option a is the trap because the plugin does work; it just hasn't been proven through the install path. Option b confuses your own marketplace, which needs no submission, with Anthropic's directory.

stem: Your group has three plugins to share: one wraps an internal API for the whole company, one is general enough for any Claude user, and one is a client-engagement build full of client-specific hooks and internal servers. Which two channel-and-readiness pairings fit?

choices.text: Internal-API plugin → your own marketplace in a private repo; ready once it validates and installs from a local marketplace
choices.reason: Correct: a `marketplace.json` in a private repository lets anyone who can clone it install by name and get updates, and the pre-release checks are validation and a local-marketplace install.

choices.text: General-purpose plugin → Anthropic's directory; ready once it validates locally and you've checked which components load outside Claude Code
choices.reason: Correct: one directory listing reaches people on claude.ai, in Cowork and in Claude Code; before submitting, validate locally and check the component support table, since some components are Claude Code-only.

choices.text: Engagement build → Anthropic's directory as-is; ready once the README explains the client context
choices.reason: A directory listing reaches the public on claude.ai, Cowork and Claude Code; hooks and servers tied to one client's network serve nobody there, and a README doesn't change that.

choices.text: Internal-API plugin → a `.zip` emailed to every engineer; ready once it loads with `--plugin-dir` on one laptop
choices.reason: Sending a folder or `.zip` gives no updates: people keep loading the copy you sent, so every fix means re-sending it to everyone.

choices.text: General-purpose plugin → `claude-plugins-official` via the developer portal; ready once the portal's validation passes
choices.reason: `claude-plugins-official` doesn't take submissions through the directory portal; listings there go through an Anthropic partner contact.

takeaway: Match the channel to the audience, then prove readiness on that channel's own path: validate, install, check what loads.
explanation: Channel follows audience: a company-only tool belongs in a private-repository marketplace, and a plugin anyone could use belongs in Anthropic's directory. Readiness is whatever that channel's install path needs: validation plus a local-marketplace install for your own marketplace, local validation plus a component check for the directory. Option c is the trap: a build tied to one client has no public audience, and a README can't supply one.
